lesson.title: e→i & -go Verbs: pido, digo, hago, pongo
lesson.subtitle: Ordering with pido, telling with digo, doing with hago, and putting with pongo

hook.title: The 'Yo -go' Squad: Tengo, Hago, Pongo, Digo, Traigo
hook.content:
Why do five of the most important verbs in Spanish end in **-go** (or **-igo**) in the 'I' (yo) form?
• **tener** ('to have') → yo **tengo**
• **hacer** ('to do/make') → yo **hago**
• **poner** ('to put/place') → yo **pongo**
• **decir** ('to say/tell', also e→i!) → yo **digo** (tú dices, él dice, nosotros decimos)
• **traer** ('to bring') → yo **traigo**!
And remember from Topic 26: because the subjunctive is built from the **yo** form, that **g** stays across the entire subjunctive (tenga, haga, ponga, diga, traiga)!

pattern.title: The e→i Boot in -ir Verbs: Pedir (Pido, Pides, Pide, Pedimos)
pattern.content: Alongside e→ie and o→ue, a special group of **-ir** verbs (like **pedir** 'to ask for / order' and **decir** 'to say/tell') raises stressed **e** to **i**: yo **pido**, tú **pides**, él/ella/usted **pide**, nosotros **pedimos**, ellos **piden**!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: pido, digo, hago, pongo, traigo, tengo
exercises.meaning: I order / ask for (pedir: e→i), I say / tell (decir: -go + e→i), I do / make (hacer: -go), I put / place (poner: -go), I bring (traer: -igo), I have (tener: -go)
exercises.explanation: The -go squad (tengo, hago, pongo, digo, traigo) anchors 1st-person singular and the entire present subjunctive!

exercises.prompt: Build 'I order / I ask for' (1st person singular of pedir, with e→i):
exercises.explanation: pedir raises e to i under stress: pido, pides, pide.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I put the book on the table' (using poner)?
options: Pongo el libro en la mesa
exercises.target_answer: Pongo el libro en la mesa
exercises.meaning: I put the book on the table
exercises.explanation: 1st person singular of poner is pongo; en means both 'in' and 'on'!

exercises.prompt: Assemble in Spanish: 'I always tell the truth':
Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Pido un café y pongo el libro en la mesa
exercises.target_answer: Pido un café y pongo el libro en la mesa
exercises.meaning: I order a coffee and I put the book on the table
cues: I order a coffee: Pido un café
and I put the book: y pongo el libro
on the table: en la mesa
exercises.explanation: Pido un café y pongo el libro en la mesa.

summary.outcome: Conjugate pedir (pido, pides, pide) and the -go verbs (tengo, hago, pongo, digo, traigo).

use_example.german: Pido un café, digo la verdad y pongo la llave en la mesa.
use_example.english: I order a coffee, I tell the truth, and I put the key on the table.

summary.takeaway: Learn the five -go verbs together: tengo, hago, pongo, digo, traigo.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next branch ([5121] Tapas, Mesa & Comida): step into a Spanish restaurant and order like a local!

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'What are you doing today? (¿Qué haces hoy?)'
twist.explanation: ¿Qué haces hoy? (only yo has the -g-: yo hago, tú haces, él hace!).

pedir.english_meaning: to ask for, to order (pido: I order/ask for)
pedir.shift_rule: Boot verb e → i (pido, pides, pide, pedimos)
pedir.context_translation: I want to order a coffee.
pedir.etymology_derivation: Latin petere ('to seek/ask for') — English petition and appetite. Needs no 'for'!

decir.english_meaning: to say, to tell (digo: I say/tell)
decir.shift_rule: Latin dīcere (-go verb: digo, dices, dice)
decir.etymology_derivation: Latin dīcere — English dictate, diction, predict.

hacer.context_translation: I want to make a reservation.
hacer.etymology_derivation: Latin facere shifted initial f- to silent h- in Spanish: hacer. English keeps the f in fact and factory.

poner.english_meaning: to put, to place (pongo: I put)
poner.shift_rule: Root of the -poner family (proponer, suponer, componer)
poner.context_phrase: Pongo el libro en la mesa.
poner.context_translation: I put the book on the table.
poner.etymology_derivation: Latin pōnere — root of propose, suppose, compose, expose.

tener.etymology_derivation: Latin tenēre ('to hold'). While other tongues used 'have' (like French avoir), Spanish promoted 'hold' (tener) to main possession.

tengo.etymology_derivation: Latin teneō developed an epenthetic velar g: tengo.

traer.context_translation: Will you bring me the bill, please?
traer.etymology_derivation: Latin trahere ('to pull/draw', English tractor, attract, distract).

verdad.etymology_derivation: Latin vēritātem gives English 'verity' and Spanish verdad.

mesa.context_translation: I want to reserve a table.
mesa.etymology_derivation: Latin mēnsa ('table') gave Spanish la mesa — which English borrowed in the American Southwest for a flat-topped 'table' mountain!

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → Spanish café. An international word shared across Europe.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.
